seoTitle: Wix vs Squarespace: Best Alternatives Compared (2026)
metaDescription: Comparing Wix, Squarespace, GoDaddy, Shopify, WordPress, and more? This breakdown helps you pick the right website builder.
intro: Choosing a website builder means weighing features, pricing, and ease of use across a crowded field of options, and the honest answer changes depending on what you're actually building. This comparison looks at what it's really like to work inside Wix's editor and pricing page, then walks through where WordPress and Shopify pull ahead for their own specific use cases — a blog-and-content site versus a serious online store. Rather than repeating marketing claims, this guide grounds each platform in its real interface and real pricing tiers, so you can judge them the way you'd judge them after actually signing up.

steps.heading: See what building in Wix actually looks like
steps.body: Wix's editor opens with Site, Settings, Dev Mode, Hire a Professional, and Help across the top, and a left rail of block-adding tools running from a big plus icon down to layers, pages, text, and design panels. A live example site called "LearnLearn.games" shows the layout in progress — a top nav with Home, Games, Community, About, and Contact, a large "+ Add Section" button for building the page section by section, and a Quick Edit shortcut hovering over the active block. Notice too that Wix flags an available domain ("learnlearngames.com is available") right in the toolbar and offers to connect it immediately — a small touch that keeps domain setup from becoming a separate task you forget about.

image.caption: Wix's drag-and-drop editor mid-build on a site called LearnLearn.games, with an "+ Add Section" prompt, a Quick Edit shortcut, and a domain-connection banner in the toolbar.

steps.heading: Check what each Wix tier actually includes
steps.body: Wix's pricing page lines up five plans side by side: Free at $0 with no credit card required, Light at $17/mo for "the basics," Core at $29/mo aimed at audience engagement, Business at $39/mo (marked Recommended) adding standard eCommerce and scheduling, and Business Elite at $159/mo for full-scale operations with unlimited storage and 100 site collaborators. The feature checkmarks make the actual gaps clear rather than leaving you to guess: Free and Light both lack e-commerce and services scheduling, Core adds basic eCommerce but not standard, and only Business and above unlock accepting payments properly. If your site needs to take payments at all, Light and Core are effectively off the table regardless of how appealing their price looks.

image.caption: Wix's five pricing tiers side by side — Free, Light, Core, Business, and Business Elite — with checkmarked features showing exactly which plan unlocks payments, eCommerce, and scheduling.

steps.heading: Where Squarespace still wins
steps.body: Squarespace's pitch has always been fewer, more polished templates rather than Wix's fully open canvas — you trade some layout freedom for a design that's harder to make look amateurish by accident. That's the core trade-off worth understanding before comparing prices line by line: Wix optimizes for control and Squarespace optimizes for a curated result, and neither is objectively better, only better for a specific kind of user. Someone comfortable fiddling with sections and spacing will prefer Wix's editor shown above; someone who wants strong defaults and fewer decisions typically prefers Squarespace's more guided setup.

steps.heading: Consider WordPress if content is the priority
steps.body: WordPress.com's homepage makes its positioning obvious the moment you open the Products menu — WordPress Hosting, WordPress for Agencies, an AI Website Builder, Website Builder, Create a Blog, Newsletter, Professional Email, Website Design Services, Commerce, and WordPress Studio are all listed as distinct products rather than tiers of one plan. The headline promises "Unmetered traffic, site recovery, dev tools, and expert support," backed by a 4.5-star rating across 2,000+ reviews and a dashboard preview showing uptime (99.999%), backup status, and server details like PHP version and caching. This is a fundamentally different pitch from Wix or Squarespace — WordPress leans into content publishing, developer control, and hosting infrastructure, which is exactly why it remains the default choice for blogs and content-heavy sites even as page builders get more visual.

image.caption: WordPress.com's homepage with its Products menu open, listing Hosting, AI Website Builder, Newsletter, and Commerce as separate offerings, next to a dashboard preview showing uptime and backups.

steps.heading: Consider Shopify if selling is the priority
steps.body: Shopify's marketing page makes its commerce-first identity clear with three side-by-side pitches: "Sell on every channel" (with logos for eBay, Pinterest, TikTok, Instagram, Amazon, Google, and YouTube), "Sell face to face" through Shopify POS to keep online and in-store sales in sync, and "Sell to 250M+ shoppers with Shop" via the Shop app's pre-verified shopper base. A checkout preview shown alongside displays a stored Visa card and an order summary total, underscoring that payment handling is baked into the core product rather than bolted on. If your site's primary job is selling physical or digital products across multiple channels, Shopify's multichannel integration is built for exactly that in a way Wix and Squarespace's more general commerce tools aren't.

image.caption: Shopify's homepage highlighting multichannel selling (eBay, Pinterest, TikTok, Amazon, Google, YouTube), in-person sales via Shopify POS, and a checkout preview with a saved card.

steps.heading: Where GoDaddy, Square, and Hostinger fit
steps.body: GoDaddy, Square, and Hostinger round out this comparison as lower-friction options: GoDaddy leans on its domain-registrar roots to bundle a website with hosting you might already be paying for, Square's website builder ties in tightly with its point-of-sale hardware for businesses that already run Square in person, and Hostinger competes mainly on price for basic hosting and site-building needs. None of these three try to out-feature Wix, Squarespace, WordPress, or Shopify — they win on convenience or cost for a narrower use case, so they're worth a look mainly if you're already inside one of their ecosystems for another reason.

steps.heading: Match the platform to what you're actually building
steps.body: If you want full visual control over layout and don't mind spending time in an editor, Wix's canvas is built for that. If you want strong design defaults with less fiddling, Squarespace stays the safer pick. If content and publishing come first, WordPress's dedicated hosting and blogging tools are hard to beat. And if selling products across channels is the whole point of the site, Shopify's checkout and multichannel tools justify its more commerce-focused pricing. Pick based on the job the site needs to do, not on which platform has the flashiest demo.

faq.question: Is Wix or Squarespace better for beginners?
faq.answer: Wix's open canvas (shown above with its "+ Add Section" workflow) gives more layout freedom but more decisions to make; Squarespace's more curated templates typically get a beginner to a polished result faster with less tinkering.

faq.question: What are the best Squarespace alternatives?
faq.answer: Wix, WordPress, Shopify, GoDaddy, Square, and Hostinger each cover a different priority — Wix for design control, WordPress for content and blogging, Shopify for commerce, and GoDaddy/Square/Hostinger for convenience or cost.

faq.question: Which Wix plan do I need to accept payments?
faq.answer: Based on Wix's pricing page, Business ($39/mo) and Business Elite ($159/mo) are the tiers that unlock full payment acceptance and eCommerce — Free, Light, and Core do not.

faq.question: Which platform is best for an online store?
faq.answer: Shopify is purpose-built for selling — its homepage highlights multichannel integration (eBay, Amazon, TikTok, and more), in-person sales via Shopify POS, and built-in checkout, which goes further than the general commerce tools in Wix or Squarespace.

faq.question: Why would someone choose WordPress over a drag-and-drop builder?
faq.answer: WordPress.com separates its offerings into distinct products — Hosting, an AI Website Builder, Newsletter, Commerce — and backs them with infrastructure details like uptime and backup status, which appeals to sites where content publishing and developer control matter more than visual drag-and-drop editing.
